Q: Oracle, PL/SQL and Java A:

First of all: use IntelliJ community edition. Don't use Visual Studio Code. I don't know why people default to that nowadays, it's not built for Java programming. You'll slow yourself down trying.

You can't just roll object oriented programming out of your sleeve in such a short time, it's just not going to happen. People go to school for years to learn that and even then they're absolute novices at it.

So I wouldn't waste your time trying and failing. Focus on writing a simple Java program that does database CRUD stuff and dumps it in a shell. That is already hard enough as you'll have to learn how to connect to a database too, and manage connections and statements. You'll have to learn what a basic class is to store data in it, you'll have to learn how to write a main and run a program, you'll have to learn how to setup a JDBC URL to connect to the database of your choice. You'll have to learn how to work with arrays to store multiple results from a resultset. You'll have to learn how to do a loop or "iterate". You'll have to learn what a "PreparedStatement" is to know how to prevent SQL injections.

I fully expect your first program to use the 'static' keyword for pretty much everything you do which, to be honest, is absolute amateur hour that does not look good on the usual job interview. To move beyond that you'll have to learn how to create objects from classes and call methods on them. I wouldn't go too deep with this; stay away from topics such as inheritance as that is a very deep rabbit hole which will cost you a lot of time and practice to understand properly. You don't have that time.

Java has a concept of "packages". I would really avoid that for your first programs and just put everything in one package.

Q: Should I implement UserDetails directly in my User entity or create a separate UserPrincipal class in Spring Security? A:

This is a general design question, and both approaches are valid. Which one is better depends on your real context.

If the User class has few attributes and is a rather simple model, having it to directly implement UserDetails may lead to simpler code with less classes. And simpler means easier to maintain...

On the other hand, if the User class has many model level interaction (beside authentication and authorizations) having it to directly implement UserDetails can bring unnecessary coupling between the model and SpringSecurity. And unnecessary coupling could be the hell for subsequent technical evolutions.

You know your model complexity, the expected time of life of your application, and the probability and changes in technical approaches. I don't. So I cannot go further than giving you some general rules...

Q: Are there any risks/downsides to putting emojis in code? A:

In terms of risks, there aren't really any real ones. If you use them in comments they'll be removed/ignored at runtime anyway so performance-wise there's no issues.

The main issue that you could run into is that some Linux distros DO NOT support emojis, so they'd fallback to some standard Unicode character (generically a white rectangle with a cross through the middle), which could make comments harder to understand.
